いく か どうか — Do We Go or Not?

You put questions “inside” a sentence: “I don’t know whether…” (～か どうか) and “I don’t know when / where / who…” (question word + ～か); at the end of August, Mihai is waiting for his N4 result, and the family wonders whether to travel to Japan, with a baby, for the anniversary of Fumiko’s teahouse.
to let someone know, to inform
pulling up to stand while holding on to something (babies)
to take time off, to be absent
I’ll check whether the result is out.
Do you know when the result comes out?
We’re torn about whether to go to Japan.
I don’t know whether the little one will like it.
Please let us know how many of you are coming.
To say “I don’t know whether…”, “I’ll check whether…”, “I wonder whether…” with ～か どうか (plain form + か どうか; no だ after な-adjectives and nouns).
To put a question with a question word inside a sentence: いつ / どこ / だれ / なに / どう / いくら … + か + わからない / しって いる / おしえて ください.
To use the variants ～か ～ない か and ～か どうか は / を, and not to confuse the questioning “if / whether” (か どうか) with the conditional “if” (～ば / ～たら).
To tell a direct question from an embedded one, from かな / かしら (wondering to yourself) and from かもしれない (maybe).

A Wednesday evening at the end of August, in Cotroceni. Rosa Elena (7 months) is crawling around the living room. Ana is reading an e-mail from Fumiko; Mihai is sitting with his laptop open on the JLPT results page.
Mihai, there’s an e-mail from Mrs Fumiko. About the teahouse’s 50th anniversary.
“We will hold the celebration on the first Saturday of April next year. Please let us know whether you can come.”
The beginning of April… Right in cherry blossom season.
And it also says: “Please also tell us how many of you are coming and roughly when you will arrive in Kyoto.”
Mihai, are you listening? Are you looking at the results page again?
Sorry. I can’t get it out of my head: is the result out yet?
Do you know when it comes out?
It only says “at the end of August”. I don’t know whether it’s today, tomorrow or next week.
(Laughing) Looking every day won’t make it come out sooner. Let’s talk about Kyoto instead. We have to decide whether we’re going.
I’d like to go, but… I’m worried whether Rosa Elena can manage fifteen hours on a plane.
As a doctor, what do you think?
At about one year old, she’ll be fine. If you give her milk during take-off and landing, her ears are less likely to hurt. But if she cries, the people around us…
What we want matters more than what the people around us think, doesn’t it?
You’re right. But I don’t even know yet whether I can take a whole week off work.
Why don’t you ask Dr Ionescu?
Yes. And I’d like to ask Grandpa too. We’re going to pick up the little stool on Saturday.
Good idea. I wonder what Grandpa will say.
Ah! Rosa Elena, no! Don’t hit the laptop!
(Looking at the screen) …The page is gone. Now I don’t know whether the result was out or not.
(Laughing) She wants to know the result quickly too.

ka-dō-ka: the “o” in どう is long (do-o). Don’t pause between か and どうか: say them together, almost like one word, and let your voice fall at the end, not rise — it isn’t a direct question.
gō-ka-ku: long “o”. go-ju-s-shū-ne-n: っ is a short stop before “shū”, and the “u” in “shū” is long. Count the beats: go-ju-(stop)-shu-u-ne-n.
hi-kō-ki: the “i” in “hi” is barely heard (between “h” and “k”), almost “h’kōki”. ri-ri-ku: the “r” is tapped lightly twice, like a soft “l” (or like the “tt” in American “butter”).

When a yes/no question goes inside another sentence (“I don’t know WHETHER he’s coming”), Japanese uses the plain form + か どうか. どうか means roughly “or not”. It is followed by a verb such as わからない (I don’t know), しらない, しらべる (I check), たしかめる, きく (I ask), きめる (I decide), まよう (I’m torn), おしえて ください.
plain form + か どうか
no だ + か どうか
After な-adjectives and nouns you do NOT put だ: ✗ しずか だ か どうか → ✓ しずか か どうか. And inside you use the PLAIN form, even if the sentence is polite: ✓ いく か どうか わかりません (✗ いきます か どうか).

The variant ～か ～ない か says the same thing, a little more colloquially: いく か いかない か、まだ きめて いない (we haven’t decided yet whether we’re going or not). You can also put particles after か どうか: ～か どうか を しらべる, ～か どうか は あした きめる (as for whether…, we’ll decide tomorrow).

English uses one little word, “if”, for two different things! “I don’t know IF he’s coming” (embedded question) = くる か どうか わからない. “IF he comes, I’ll be happy” (condition) = きたら うれしい / くれば うれしい. Ask yourself: can I replace “if” with “whether”? If so → か どうか.
2. Question word + ～か: “I don’t know when / where / who…”
When the embedded question has a question word (いつ, どこ, だれ, なに, どう, どうして, いくら, なんにん, どの…), you NO longer add どうか: you just put か after the plain form.
What we want matters more than what the people around us think.
I don’t know why she’s crying.
With どうして / なぜ you often use の か (explanation): どうして ないて いる の か. With a noun or a な-adjective, again no だ: だれ の いす か わからない (I don’t know whose chair it is), どれ が いちばん だいじ か.
Don’t mix them up: with a question word → only か (✗ いつ でる か どうか). Without a question word → か どうか (or ～か ～ない か).
3. Direct question, embedded question, かな / かしら, かもしれない
Four ways of talking about something uncertain, all with か, but not the same:
you say what you don’t know / what you’re checking
you wonder to yourself, out loud
Ana combines two: おじいさん なら、なんて いう かしら (“I wonder what Grandpa will say” — she’s wondering to herself). Gheorghe: いきたい か どうか、それ だけ を かんがえなさい (“just think about whether you want to go”).
4. Review: verbs that take an embedded question
I don’t know whether we’re going.
I’ll ask whether I can take time off.
I’m torn about whether to go.
Tell me how many of you are coming.
I don’t remember where I put it.
Did you notice? ～て みる (ch. 27) fits nicely here too: きいて みる (“I’ll try asking”), しらべて みる (“I’ll check and see”).
5. Culture: with a baby in Japan
Japan is quite a friendly country for parents of small children, if you know a few words:
room for breastfeeding and feeding the baby (in big stations, shops, airports)
priority seats on trains and buses (also for people with small children)
stroller; on crowded trains you fold it or keep it close to you

There is no direct flight from Romania to Japan: you usually change planes once and land at Kansai Airport (near Osaka), from where you take the train to Kyoto. Including the layover, the journey takes about 15–18 hours.
Mihai’s advice is the same one doctors give: during take-off and landing, give the baby milk or water. Swallowing equalises the pressure in the ears, so it hurts less.

ばら の いす — The Little Stool with the Rose
On a Saturday at the end of August, the three of them set off by car for the village. It was the day Rosa Elena went to the village for the first time.
“More than three hours in the car… I’m worried whether she’ll cry or not.”
But Rosa Elena fell asleep as soon as the car started moving and didn’t wake up even once until they reached the village.
“I turned around I don’t know how many times to make sure she was breathing,” Mihai laughed.
Grandpa was waiting for them in front of the house, wearing his best jacket. Sura was there beside him too.
When Mihai handed Rosa Elena to him, Grandpa took her gently in his arms, with trembling hands.
“I couldn’t sleep last night, I kept wondering whether I’d be able to hold her. …She weighs about as much as Mihai did when he was a baby.”
Rosa Elena stared at the unfamiliar face, then suddenly grabbed Grandpa by the nose and squealed with laughter.
Grandpa laughed too, his face full of wrinkles: “Ileana, are you watching? Our great-granddaughter grabbed me by the nose.”
Just then, the old door creaked open in the wind. Sura snorted softly.
When Mihai stood in front of Sura holding Rosa Elena, the mare slowly brought her big head closer. They thought the little girl would be scared, but she patted Sura’s muzzle with her tiny hands.
“She isn’t afraid of anything. She must take after her great-grandpa,” Grandpa said, delighted — meaning himself.
When they went into the house, Grandpa brought a little stool from the workshop.
It had the same shape as Mihai’s stool by the stove, only a little smaller. The cherry wood glowed in its warm colour.
A rose was carved into the seat.
“I heard from Elena that Rosa means rose. Whether the little one will like it, that I don’t know…”
When Ana put Rosa Elena down on the floor, she crawled straight over to the stool.
Then she grabbed hold of it and, wobbling, pulled herself up to stand.
“She’s standing!” Mihai and Ana cried at the same time. It was the first time she had pulled herself up holding on to something.
Rosa Elena stroked the rose with her tiny fingers and said, “Aaah.”
“No need to ask whether she likes it,” said Ana, and Grandpa smiled, his eyes crinkling.
By the stove the big stool and the little one were placed side by side.
In the afternoon three old women from the village came with pies and cozonac (sweet bread). They were the very same old women who had learned from Mrs Fumiko how to make tea.
The youngest of them asked whether the tea teacher from Japan was well. “If the little one goes to Kyoto, give her my regards.”
The old women took turns holding Rosa Elena and kept on talking: “The spitting image of Mihai!” “No, the eyes are Ana’s.”
That evening, in front of the stove, Ana told him about Mrs Fumiko’s e-mail.
“Next spring, the teahouse in Kyoto turns 50. But we still can’t decide whether to go.”
Mihai counted on his fingers: “Whether Rosa Elena can cope with a long flight. Whether I can take time off work. Whether we have enough money…”
Grandpa was silent for a while, looking at the fire in the stove.
“When I was young, I didn’t even know whether I’d still be alive tomorrow.”
“If you keep thinking only about whether you can, you never do anything. Just think about whether you want to go.”
“…We want to go.” Ana’s and Mihai’s voices overlapped again.
“Then go. While the people waiting for you are still healthy.”
Then Grandpa added, a little embarrassed: “Take a photo for me. I want to see with my own eyes whether that spoon was really used.”
Saying this, Grandpa put another log on the fire. The fire crackled.
That night, Mihai couldn’t fall asleep for a long time. Beside him, Ana whispered: “Tell me, do you think Grandpa is right?” “Yes. We were only looking for reasons why we couldn’t.”
The next day, on the way home, in the car, the two of them decided: “Let’s go. To Kyoto.”
As they said goodbye, Grandpa stroked Rosa Elena’s head: “Next time, come on your own two feet.”
Back in Bucharest, Mihai phoned Dr Ionescu and asked whether he could take a week off in the spring.
Dr Ionescu looked at the calendar and laughed: “I’m afraid a week won’t be enough. Take ten days.”
That evening, Ana wrote her reply to Mrs Fumiko.
At the end she wrote “The three of us will be delighted to come” and pressed the send button.
On the morning of the last day of August, Mihai got up earlier than usual.
All that week he had checked every morning whether the result was out.
He opened the laptop and typed in his exam number. “It’s out!” But before he pressed the button, his finger froze.
“Ana, won’t you look for me? I’m scared to see by myself whether I passed.”
Ana, with Rosa Elena in her arms, leaned towards the screen. For a while she said nothing. Mihai’s heart was pounding.
“…Hey, Mihai. This word, «gōkaku», what does it mean again?”
“What?” When Mihai looked at the screen, it said in big letters: “PASSED”.
One hundred and twenty-eight points out of one hundred and eighty. Even in listening, his weak spot, he had comfortably cleared the pass mark.
Mihai jumped up from his chair and hugged Ana and Rosa Elena together.
They cheered so loudly that Mrs Doina next door knocked on the door: “What’s happened? Has Rozița walked?”
When she heard why, Mrs Doina gave Mihai a hearty slap on the back and laughed: “I never worried for a second about whether you’d pass!”
When they called Elena, she couldn’t say anything for a while. Then she said in a tearful voice: “Let Grandpa know right away too.”
Rosa Elena, without knowing what had happened, clapped her hands and laughed.
A message from Ioana came right away too: “I passed N3! How did you do?”
From Sakura in Hiroshima came: “Congratulations, big brother! Congratulations to Hana-chan too!”
“Why Hana-chan too?” Mihai asked, and Sakura replied: “Well, didn’t she sleep nicely so as not to disturb your studying?”
Mihai and Ana looked at each other and burst out laughing. The chewed workbook on the desk seemed to be laughing too.
Outside the window, the end-of-summer wind was blowing. “Well, next up: Kyoto.”
